title: Law court
description: The three Acts you need: data protection, computer misuse, and copyright, and which one applies.
kicker: 1.6 Ethical, legal, cultural and environmental impacts  |  Lesson 3
subtitle: OCR J277 Paper 1  |  Computer systems
intro: The three Acts you need: data protection, computer misuse, and copyright, and which one applies.

stations.name: Data Protection Act 2018
bullets: Governs how organisations collect, store and use personal data.
Data must be used fairly and lawfully, for a stated purpose, kept accurate, kept no longer than needed, and kept secure.
People have rights: to see their data, to correct it, and in many cases to have it deleted.
stations.challenge: State three things the Data Protection Act requires of an organisation.

tasks.q: Which of these are requirements of the Data Protection Act 2018? Select all that apply.
opts: Data must be accurate and up to date
Data must not be kept longer than necessary
Data must be collected for a stated purpose
Data must be stored in the UK only
Data must be printed once a year
correct: Data must be accurate and up to date
Data must not be kept longer than necessary
Data must be collected for a stated purpose
tasks.fb: Location is not a requirement; the safeguards travel with the data.

tasks.q: A company keeps customer records for 25 years with no reason. Which Act is breached?
a: The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
None: keeping data is always allowed
tasks.fb: Data must not be kept longer than necessary.

stations.name: Computer Misuse Act 1990
bullets: Created to deal with hacking, which no earlier law covered.
Three main offences: unauthorised access; unauthorised access with intent to commit a further offence; unauthorised modification of data.
Access without permission is an offence even if nothing is changed or taken.
stations.challenge: Explain why guessing a friend's password and logging in is an offence even if you change nothing.
stations.fact: The Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes it an offence to...

tasks.q: A student uses a teacher's login to read a mark sheet, changing nothing. Is this an offence?
a: Yes: unauthorised access is an offence on its own
No, because it was a school computer
tasks.fb: Access without permission is the first offence in the Act.

tasks.q: The same student then changes their grade. What has now happened?
a: A second, more serious offence: unauthorised modification of data
It becomes a privacy matter only
tasks.fb: Modification carries heavier penalties than access alone.

stations.name: Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
bullets: Protects the creator of original work: software, music, film, writing, images.
Copying, sharing or selling without permission infringes copyright.
It applies automatically the moment work is created: no registration needed.
stations.challenge: Explain why using an image from a web search in a book you sell is a problem.
stations.fact: The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 protects...

tasks.q: Someone uploads a film they bought to a sharing site. Which Act have they breached?
a: The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
tasks.fb: Buying a copy does not buy the right to distribute it.

tasks.q: Why is this Act constantly having to adapt?
a: Copying digital work is effortless and global, which the Act was not written for
Because copyright expires after one year
tasks.fb: Streaming, sampling and AI training all raise questions it never anticipated.

stations.name: Which Act applies?
bullets: Personal data misused or leaked: Data Protection Act.
Access, hacking or changing data without permission: Computer Misuse Act.
Copying or sharing someone's creative work: Copyright, Designs and Patents Act.
stations.challenge: Sort six scenarios into the right Act, with a reason for each.
stations.fact: To decide which Act applies, ask...

tasks.q: Which Act does each situation fall under?
items: A hospital emails patient records to the wrong address
A pupil logs in as a teacher to see exam papers
A shop sells copied games at a market stall
A company sells customer emails without telling them
Someone plants malware that deletes files
A website uses a photographer's pictures without asking
tasks.fb: Personal data, unauthorised access, or someone's creative work: that's the decision.

stations.name: Other legislation
bullets: Freedom of Information allows anyone to request information held by public bodies, such as what a council spent.
It covers public information, not personal data about individuals.
Health and safety, equality and consumer law also apply to technology.
stations.challenge: Which law would you use to find out what a council paid for a new traffic system?

tasks.q: A resident wants to know what the council spent on a cycle lane. Which law helps?
tasks.fb: Public money, public body, public information.

tasks.q: Can someone use Freedom of Information to get a named employee's salary and address?
a: No: personal data is protected, not released
Yes, all council data is public
tasks.fb: The two laws work together: openness about the organisation, protection for individuals.

stations.name: Answering legal questions
bullets: Name the Act in full, including the year, then state the relevant principle.
Say which part of the situation breaches it.
If more than one Act applies, say so: many real cases involve two.
stations.challenge: Write a full answer to: a worker copies the customer database before leaving for a rival.

tasks.q: A worker copies the customer database and takes it to a rival firm. Which Acts are involved?
a: The Data Protection Act, for misuse of personal data, and the Computer Misuse Act, for unauthorised access
tasks.fb: Real cases often engage more than one Act.

tasks.q: Which is the better exam answer?
a: This breaches the Computer Misuse Act 1990, because accessing data without permission is an offence

final.name: Final challenge: name the Act
final.intro: Nine cases have reached the court. Tap the star and decide which Act each one falls under.

tasks.q: Which Act applies to each case?
items: A charity leaves donor records on an unencrypted laptop
A teenager breaks into a school network to look around
A site streams films without the studio's permission
An employee sells patient details to a newspaper
A student sells copies of a textbook as a PDF
A shop keeps CCTV of customers for ten years with no reason
Someone guesses a colleague's password and reads their email
An app uses a song in its adverts without a licence
tasks.fb: Personal data, unauthorised access, or creative work. Name the Act and the year.

info: The Computer Misuse Act was passed after two hackers who broke into a mailbox system were acquitted, because no existing law covered what they had done.
Serious data protection breaches can be fined up to 4% of a company's worldwide turnover, which is why boards now pay attention.
In the UK, copyright in a literary or musical work lasts for the creator's lifetime plus 70 years.
Limited copying for criticism, review, news reporting or education can be allowed under fair dealing, but the rules are narrower than most people assume.
Freedom of Information covers councils, schools, the NHS and government departments, not private companies.
Every piece of software you use came with a licence setting out what you may do with it. Section 7 of this topic is about what those licences say.
